newsitem.title: FRANCE: French flag-waving chills Paris bourse.
newsitem.headline: French flag-waving chills Paris bourse.

text.p: The French government's reluctance to let companies such as insolvent airline Air Liberte and car parts maker Valeo fall into foreign hands has taken some of the fizz out of the Paris bourse.

Market operators say the conservative government's interventionism is capping share prices by thwarting cross-border takeovers and also undercuts its goal of raising the Paris stock market's profile in Europe.
"We're returning to a kind of Gaullist interventionism which may have been justified in the past but absolutely isn't today," said portfolio manager Christian Mariais at brokerage Oddo.
"Whether you're talking about (nickel producer) Eramet or Valeo, this policy leaves a very poor impression on investors," Mariais said.

In the case of car parts supplier Valeo, put in play at the start of the year by Italian industrialist Carlo De Benedetti who wanted to sell his 28 percent block, the government backed the French car industry in insisting on a French buyer.
Its stance and a boycott threat by France's two carmakers dissuaded foreign suitors, reported to include U.S. giants General Motors Corp. and TRW Inc., from launching buyout offers.

France is having a harder time deterring British Airways, which wants to expand operations in France by buying insolvent Air Liberte. The daily Le Monde said Prime Minister Alain Juppe had told the finance ministry to seek "a national solution".
And President Jacques Chirac is reported to have intervened personally to ensure that electronics and defence giant Thomson SA, slated for privatisation, is kept out of British hands.

"Their preference is always for the French solution so the best offer doesn't prevail -- it's a more nationalistic than capitalist policy," said Jacques Chahine, chairman of bourse forecasting firm Jacques Chahine Finance.
But he said France had come a long way in accepting through a new wave of privatisations begun in 1993 that the state should relinquish direct ownership of companies.
The Gaullist-led government justifies its activist policy as a means of preserving France's industrial base and jobs.

"When it comes to preserving the industrial fabric, jobs in France and fighting against needless relocations, the state must retain a capacity to intervene," Industry Minister Franck Borotra said in a speech last week.

Traders lament the developments, saying speculative trading in companies likely to be bought out in industry consolidations or restructurings had injected some excitement into a market dogged by weak economic and profit growth.
"With no real recovery taking place in France, people look at the government's approach and it makes them nervous," said Jean-Pierre Filbien, chief trader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The latest blow to investors came when the government announced its intention this month to enact anti-takeover laws.

"There are various channels that could be pursued to better anticipate, better detect attacks -- by giving companies more time to carry out capital increases when under threat," Chirac told Valeurs Actuelles magazine.
Traders say foreign investors, who represent more than half of Paris bourse activity, are especially unnerved at the prospect of state-sanctioned "poison pill" defences.
Even investors holding shares with almost no speculative potential are concerned about government intervention.

Last week, state-owned Eramet's minority shareholders saw their holdings hit a year low on concerns that the government was backing a rival mining project in nickel-rich New Caledonia to pacify separatists in the French territory in the Pacific.

Mariais said he believed the government's intervention was a big factor in the bourse's weak performance relative to British, German and U.S. stockmarkets which are trading around historic highs. The bourse last set a record high in February of 1994.
"I would say a big part of its underperformance is due to the government's interventionist policy," Mariais said.
